# Reference: measurement, frequency and components {#sec-ref-frequency}

**Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis** holds the steps that turn
waveforms into numbers: ERP Measure for time-domain scores; Fourier, Welch,
Spectral Measure and RESS for the frequency domain; Covariance and Cross
Correlation for relations between channels; and Source Estimate, which
stores a cortical inverse for later statistics.

## ERP Measure {#sec-tr-measure}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > ERP Measure · averaged or
epoched → the same, with measurements · `Measure`*

Turns a window on a waveform into a number. A table of **measurement
windows**, each a time range and a way of reducing it to a value, is
evaluated for every bin and every selected channel. On an average this
gives one value per bin; on epoched data the same windows give one value per
trial, which the statistical report's single-trial models use
(@sec-statistics). The waveforms are not changed.

![**ERP Measure** with the N400 windows of the worked example: mean amplitude and 50% area latency over 300 to 500 ms at CPz.](images/measure-dialog.png){#fig-measure-dialog}

| Measure | Reports | Unit |
|-----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|-------------|
| **Mean Amplitude** | the mean of the waveform over the window | µV |
| **Peak** | the most extreme sample of the chosen polarity, and its latency | µV, ms |
| **Area**, whole window | the integral over the window, in the chosen area mode | µV·ms |
| **Area**, peak band | the integral over a band of **Width** ms centred on the peak, and the peak's amplitude and latency | µV·ms, µV, ms |
| **Fractional Peak Latency** | the time, before the peak, at which the waveform reaches **Fraction** of the peak amplitude, interpolated between samples | ms |
| **Fractional Area Latency** | the time that divides the window's area at **Fraction**, interpolated between samples | ms |

: The measures of ERP Measure. {#tbl-measures}

| Column | Values | Used by |
|-----------------|-------------------------------------------------------|--------------------|
| **Label** | a name, best unique | all |
| **Start**, **Stop** | the window, in ms, snapped to the nearest sample | all |
| **Polarity** | Positive, Negative | peak-based measures |
| **Width** | 0 for the whole window, or a band in ms | Area |
| **Local pts** | 0 for the absolute extreme; *N* for a peak more extreme than its *N* neighbours on each side | peak-based measures |
| **Fraction** | between 0 and 1 | fractional latencies |
| **Area mode** | Signed, Rectified, Positive, Negative | Area |
| **Baseline** | an interval such as `-100 0`, subtracted before measuring | all |
| **Reference channel** | find the peak once, on this channel, and read every channel at its latency | Peak, band Area |
| **Channels** | a list, each measured separately; `{Pz POz CPz}` pools a region; blank for all | all |

: The columns of the window table. {#tbl-measure-columns}

The dialog greys the columns a row's measure does not use. **Derived
channels** can be defined in a `let` field as in Derive Channels
(@sec-tr-derivechannels), though deriving them in that step is the better
choice. **Save** and **Load** write and read a window set as an `.alm` file;
Load adds to the table, so a battery can be assembled from several files.
Ready-made sets for P1, N170, P2, MMN, visual MMN, N2, P300, N400, LPP, LRP
and ERN are in the library (@sec-library), where Load opens the first time.
Each says where its window and site come from and how it compares with that
source: the P300 and LRP sets match ERP CORE [@kappenman2021], the N400 set
takes its window but measures at Cz where ERP CORE uses CPz, and the MMN set
uses 150 to 250 ms where ERP CORE uses 125 to 225 ms. Choose windows before
looking at your data, and from a source you can cite.

When a Measure result is drawn, the measurements are marked on the
waveforms: a dot at a peak, the area shaded, a level line at a mean, and a
drop line at a fractional latency.

### Choosing a measure

The choice of measure matters as much as the choice of window
[@luckApplied; @luck2014].

- **Mean amplitude is the default choice.** A peak is biased by noise (a
  noisier waveform has larger peaks) and by the width of the window (a wider
  window can only find a larger one), so peak amplitudes are comparable
  across conditions and groups only when both are equal. A mean over a fixed
  window has neither bias.
- **For latency, use the 50% area latency** rather than the peak latency: it
  is far less affected by noise [@kiesel2008]. Fractional peak latency is
  the usual measure of onset. Latencies of single subjects are noisy in any
  case, and jackknifing, measuring the grand averages of leave-one-out
  subsamples, is often the better approach for group differences
  [@miller1998; @kiesel2008].
- **Choose windows before looking at the effect.** A window placed where the
  difference between conditions is largest inflates the false-positive rate
  in a way no correction repairs [@luckgaspelin2017]. Take windows from the
  literature, from an orthogonal contrast (the average of all conditions), or
  test without a window at all with a cluster test
  (@sec-cluster-statistics).

**Toolbox or own code.** These are ERPLAB's measures, written in Alakazam so
that they work on its averages and grand averages, pooled channels and
reference-channel peaks, with the SME beside each value. On all ten of
Luck's N400 erpsets [@luckApplied] they match ERPLAB 13.10 to a relative
4e-8, and the latencies exactly.

## Fourier {#sec-tr-fourier}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > Fourier · epoched or
continuous → frequency domain · `Fourier`*

The discrete Fourier transform of each segment (each trial of epoched data),
tapered at its ends, in one of six units.

![**Fourier**, set to a calibrated power spectral density with a 10% Hanning taper.](images/fourier-dialog.png){#fig-fourier-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---------------------|-------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| **Units** | Volt | **Volt**, **Power**, **VoltDens**, **PowerDens**, **Complex** or **PSD** (below). |
| **Full spectrum (×2)** | on | Double the one-sided magnitude, for the folded negative frequencies. Ignored for PSD. |
| **Taper** | Hanning | The window function. |
| **Length (% of segment)** | 100 | The share of the segment that is tapered, half at each end; 100 is a full Hanning window, 10 tapers 5% at each end and leaves the rest flat. |
| **Mode**, **Resolution** | Max | **Max** uses the segment's own length, padded to a power of two; **Other** sets the frequency spacing to at most the value given, and never coarser than **Max**. |

: Fourier's options. {#tbl-fourier}

**Which unit.** The first four are magnitudes: the absolute value is taken
per segment, so the phase is discarded. **Volt** gives a sinusoid of
amplitude *A* a peak of *A*, matching BrainVision Analyzer. **Complex** keeps
the coefficients, so the phase survives. The view's **P** key shows it,
wrapped to the range -π to π and drawn as points. The phase is measured from
the segment's first sample, so a cosine that starts there at phase φ reads φ
at its frequency. It is not unwrapped across frequency: the phase of a noisy
spectrum changes independently from one frequency to the next, and unwrapping
it only piles up the ramp that comes from where the segment starts.
**PSD** is the only calibrated unit: a periodogram in units²/Hz, normalised
by the energy of the taper, whose integral over frequency equals the
signal's mean square [@welch1967], so that it can be compared with other
software and with published values. Power and PowerDens square the
amplitude convention and are kept for continuity with earlier analyses.

**The order of averaging decides what is measured.** Averaging magnitude
spectra over trials (Fourier, then Average) keeps activity that is not phase
locked: it is the **total** spectrum. Averaging complex spectra, or taking
the Fourier transform of an average, keeps only the phase-locked part: the
**evoked** spectrum. The two differ by the induced power, which is often most
of the signal. On epoched data, Fourier with PSD followed by Average is
Welch's method with the trials as its segments.

**Resolution.** The frequency resolution of a segment is the reciprocal of
its length, whatever the spacing: padding with zeros interpolates the
spectrum without resolving anything finer. A spacing coarser than the
segment supports (**Other** with a value above the reciprocal of the segment
length) would need a transform shorter than the segment, which uses only its
start. Alakazam pads to the segment's own length instead, so the whole
segment is always transformed and such a value gives the same spectrum as
**Max**.

![The PSD of the N400 epochs at Oz, averaged per bin, with the frequency bands of @sec-settings shaded beneath it and the alpha peak near 10 Hz.](images/fourier-result.jpg){#fig-fourier-result}

**Toolbox or own code.** The transform is MATLAB's `fft` with the Signal
Processing Toolbox's windows. The amplitude outputs reproduce BrainVision
Analyzer's, and the complex output lets Average form an evoked spectrum,
neither of which EEGLAB's `spectopo` or FieldTrip offers. The calibrated
**PSD** is the quantity FieldTrip's `ft_freqanalysis` computes, and matches
it to 1e-15.

## Welch PSD {#sec-tr-welch}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > Welch PSD · continuous →
frequency domain · `Welch`*

The calibrated power spectral density of a continuous recording, by Welch's
method [@welch1967]: overlapping segments, each tapered, their periodograms
averaged. A segment containing rejected samples is skipped.

![**Welch PSD** with 2 s segments overlapping by half, and a Hanning taper.](images/welch-dialog.png){#fig-welch-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|--------------|-------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| **Segment length** | 4 s | The resolution is its reciprocal: 0.25 Hz for 4 s. |
| **Overlap** | 50% | The overlap of consecutive segments; 50% is usual with a Hanning taper. |
| **Taper** | Hanning | The window function. |

: Welch's options. {#tbl-welch}

Segment length is the trade between resolution and variance: longer
segments resolve lower frequencies, more segments give a steadier estimate.
Welch refuses epoched data: there, Fourier with PSD followed by Average is
already an averaged periodogram with one segment per trial, and splitting
each trial further would spend resolution twice.

![The Welch PSD of the continuous N400 recording at Oz, 2 s segments.](images/welch-result.jpg){#fig-welch-result}

**Toolbox or own code.** MATLAB's `pwelch` computes the same spectrum, and
on clean data Welch PSD matches it exactly. It is not called because a
segment holding rejected samples would make its whole result missing, where
Welch PSD leaves that segment out.

## Spectral Measure {#sec-tr-spectralmeasure}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > Spectral Measure · epoched →
epoched, with spectral measures · `SpectralMeasure`*

Measures responses at named frequencies, for frequency tagging, steady-state
responses (SSVEP) and rapid invisible frequency tagging (RIFT)
[@norcia2015; @zhigalov2019]. For each frequency, channel and bin it reports:

| Quantity | Definition |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| **power**, **amplitude** | of the evoked (trial-averaged) complex coefficient, since a tagged response is phase-locked to the stimulation |
| **SNR** | the power at the frequency divided by the mean power at the neighbouring frequencies on each side, beyond a guard band |
| **ITC** | inter-trial phase coherence, $\lvert \frac{1}{N}\sum_n X_n/\lvert X_n\rvert \rvert$, between 0 and 1 [@tallonbaudry1996; @lachaux1999] |
| **phase** | the angle of the evoked coefficient, measured from the event (time zero), as FieldTrip measures it |
| **coherence**, **phase lag** | magnitude-squared coherence and cross phase to a reference channel such as a photodiode |

: What Spectral Measure reports. {#tbl-spectralmeasure-quantities}

Frequencies are written as expressions over named fundamentals: after
`let f1 = 60`, a row may ask for `f1`, `2*f1` (a harmonic) or `f1+f2` and
`2*f1-f2` (intermodulation terms). Each coefficient is computed by a tapered
discrete Fourier transform evaluated exactly at the requested frequency, so a
harmonic or intermodulation frequency that falls between the bins of the
epoch's own spectrum is still measured exactly. Phase is measured from the
event, so the same response reads the same phase however long before the
event the epoch starts.

**Toolbox or own code.** The transform is the Signal Processing Toolbox's
`goertzel`, the Fourier transform at a single frequency, with its `hann` and
`dpss` tapers. FieldTrip's `ft_freqanalysis` was the alternative, but it
rounds every frequency to the grid of the epoch's own spectrum, so a harmonic
or intermodulation row could not be read at its exact frequency; at a
frequency on that grid the two give the same coefficients. Amplitude, SNR and
ITC are their textbook definitions applied to those coefficients, since
neither FieldTrip nor EEGLAB has them as functions for a single frequency.
The frame-averaged coherence is FieldTrip's coherence estimator on the same
coefficients, with one difference that matters only when trials are rejected
per channel: the reference's power is taken over the same trials as the
cross-spectrum. Every one of these quantities is checked against FieldTrip
in the test suite and agrees with it to rounding.

![**Spectral Measure** on a RIFT recording: the fundamental, the reference channel, the taper and SNR settings, the coherence estimator, and one row per tagged frequency.](images/spectralmeasure-dialog.png){#fig-spectralmeasure-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|----------------------------------|--------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| **Fundamentals** | | `let` lines naming the base frequencies. |
| rows: **Label**, **Frequency**, **Channels** | | A frequency expression and the channels to measure; `{Pz POz}` pools. |
| **Reference channel** | none | The channel coherence and phase lag are computed against. |
| **Taper method**, **Multitaper tapers** | Hann, 3 | A single Hann taper, or DPSS multitapers, which average over *K* tapers to reduce variance. |
| **SNR neighbour bins**, **SNR guard bins** | 10, 1 | How many frequency bins on each side form the noise estimate, and how many next to the frequency are skipped. |
| **Coherence estimator** | Frame-averaged | See below. |
| **Window start**, **Window stop** | whole epoch | The part of each epoch analysed, to leave out the onset response. |

: Spectral Measure's options. {#tbl-spectralmeasure}

**Coherence.** Only coherence and phase lag depend on the estimator; the
single-channel quantities do not.

- **Frame-averaged** (the default) cuts the signals into overlapping frames
  (75% overlap), computes the coherence across trials in each frame at the
  exact frequency, and averages over frames. It agrees frame by frame with
  FieldTrip's sliding-window coherence (`ft_freqanalysis` with `mtmconvol`,
  then `ft_connectivityanalysis`), closely with EEGLAB's `newcrossf`, and
  with the Coherence Map and CohTopo views, so the number in a report and the
  map beside it are the same quantity.
- **Window** uses the whole analysis window as one tapered segment per trial.
  It is cheap but biased upwards, since far fewer independent samples enter
  the average: on ten RIFT recordings it read 2.4 to 2.9 times the
  frame-averaged value.
- **newcrossf** calls EEGLAB's own function, the estimator the RIFT study
  used [@dimigen2025], and can only report frequencies inside its band.
  Rejected trials are left out before the call, as the other estimators
  leave them out.

The report states which estimator was used. **Spectral & Report** on the
**Export/Report** tab collects every Spectral Measure result into a CSV and
a report (@sec-frequency-tagging).

![A RIFT recording's evoked amplitude spectrum at Oz in the 60 Hz condition, 0 to 100 Hz, with the measured frequencies marked and labelled with their SNR: the tagged 60 Hz response (SNR about 100), and a larger 50 Hz line-noise peak beside it.](images/spectralmeasure-result.jpg){#fig-spectralmeasure-result}

## RESS {#sec-tr-ress}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > RESS · epoched, with bins →
the same, with added channels · `RESS`*

Rhythmic entrainment source separation [@cohen2017]. A tagged response is
usually read from the electrode where it looks strongest, a choice that
differs between people and frequencies and is circular when made on the
response itself. RESS replaces it with a spatial filter per recording and
frequency: the weighting of all scalp channels whose power at the
stimulation frequency is largest relative to the frequencies beside it. Each
filter is added as a channel (`RESS60Hz`), so that everything downstream,
Spectral Measure's coherence to a photodiode, SNR and ITC, reads it like an
electrode.

![**RESS** for the RIFT design: one row per tagged frequency, each built from its own bins, with the reference code's filter widths.](images/ress-dialog.png){#fig-ress-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---------------------------------------|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| rows: **Label**, **Frequency**, **Build from bins** | | One component per row, built from the pooled trials of the listed bins (blank: all). |
| **Width at the frequency** | 0.5 Hz | FWHM of the narrow Gaussian filter at the frequency. |
| **Neighbours, either side** | 1 Hz | Distance of the reference frequencies. |
| **Width at the neighbours** | 1 Hz | FWHM of the filters at the neighbours. |
| **Window start**, **Window stop** | whole epoch | The samples entering the covariances, to leave out the onset response. |
| **Shrinkage of the reference** | 1% | Regularisation of the reference covariance (below). |
| **Include the mastoids** | off | Include mastoid channels among the scalp channels combined. |

: RESS's options. The defaults are those of the authors' code. {#tbl-ress}

**The method.** Two channel covariance matrices are formed from the same
samples: **S** from the data filtered narrowly at the frequency, and **R**
as the mean of the covariances at the frequency minus and plus the
neighbour distance. The generalised eigenvector of (S, R) with the largest
eigenvalue maximises the ratio of power at the frequency to power beside
it. The filters are Gaussians in the frequency domain, applied to the whole
epoch before the window is taken. The forward model (the component's scalp
map) is $S\mathbf w / (\mathbf w^\top S \mathbf w)$, and the sign is fixed so
that the largest element of the map is positive; unlike the reference code,
the weights are flipped with it, so that the component's phase, and its
phase lag to a photodiode, is not arbitrary.

**Shrinkage.** An average reference, an interpolated channel or a removed
ICA component lowers the rank of the data, and a singular R has no
well-defined generalised eigenvectors. R is therefore shrunk towards a
multiple of the identity, $(1-g)R + g\,\overline{\lambda}(R)\,I$; 0 reproduces
the article, which used full-rank data.

**Which trials.** A filter built from every condition at a frequency compares
those conditions fairly, because none had the filter fitted to it alone, as
the authors advise. The component is then computed for every trial, so it is
also applied to the bins it was not built from, and those are its null: what
the filter gives where its flicker was absent. A recording without a row's
bins gets that component as all-missing, with a note, so that every
recording keeps the same channels.

Only scalp EEG channels are combined, never eye channels, a photodiode or an
earlier component; running RESS again replaces its channels. The weights,
maps and eigenvalues are kept for the report.

![The spectrum of the 60 Hz RESS component in the same trials: SNR at 60 Hz about 460, against about 100 at Oz (@fig-spectralmeasure-result), with the 50 Hz line noise largely gone.](images/ress-result.jpg){#fig-ress-result}

**Toolbox or own code.** No toolbox implements RESS. Alakazam's follows
Cohen and Gulbinaite's own script [@cohen2017] and reproduces its filters to
ten decimals.

## Covariance {#sec-tr-covariance}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > Covariance · epoched →
channel matrix per bin · `Covariance`*

The channel-by-channel covariance or correlation matrix of each bin, over
the samples of a time window pooled across the bin's trials.

![**Covariance**: the channels, the statistic, the shrinkage, and the window.](images/covariance-dialog.png){#fig-covariance-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|------------------|--------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Channels** | all | At least two. |
| **Matrix** | Covariance | **Covariance** (µV²) or **Correlation**. |
| **Shrinkage** | Ledoit-Wolf | **Ledoit-Wolf**, or **None**. |
| **Window** start, stop | 0 to 0 (whole epoch) | The samples used, in ms. |

: Covariance's options. {#tbl-covariance}

With *p* channels, a sample covariance needs many more than *p* independent
observations to be well conditioned, and a 64-channel montage over a short
window rarely has them: the small eigenvalues come out too small or zero,
which breaks anything that later inverts the matrix. Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage
towards a scaled identity is the closed-form optimum, needs no tuning
parameter, and is always positive definite [@ledoit2004]; the condition
number before and after is reported. A correlation matrix is derived from
the shrunk covariance, in that order.

Rejected samples are handled by dropping every time point at which any
selected channel was rejected, rather than pairwise: pairwise deletion
computes each entry from a different set of samples, and the result need not
be a valid covariance matrix. The number of observations used and dropped is
shown with each matrix.

![The correlation matrix of the N400 epochs of one bin, with the number of observations used and dropped in the title. The EOG channels, at the bottom right, correlate little with the rest.](images/covariance-result.jpg){#fig-covariance-result}

**Toolbox or own code.** MATLAB's `cov` and `corrcoef` give the raw
estimate, which Covariance matches on clean data. The shrinkage, which no
MATLAB, EEGLAB or FieldTrip function offers, and the handling of rejected
samples are Alakazam's.

## Cross Correlation {#sec-tr-crosscorrelation}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > Cross Correlation · epoched
→ lag functions per bin · `CrossCorrelation`*

The Pearson correlation of each channel with a reference channel at every
lag, computed per trial and averaged over the bin's trials, with the peak
correlation and its lag. **A positive lag means the channel follows the
reference.**

![**Cross Correlation**: the reference channel, the channels, the maximum lag, the minimum number of sample pairs per lag, and the window.](images/crosscorrelation-dialog.png){#fig-crosscorrelation-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|----------------------------|--------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| **Reference channel** | | Required. |
| **Channels** | all | The channels correlated with it. |
| **Maximum lag** | 200 ms | The range of lags, either side. |
| **Minimum sample pairs per lag** | 20 | A lag with fewer valid pairs is left empty. |
| **Window** start, stop | 0 to 0 (whole epoch) | The samples used, in ms. |

: Cross Correlation's options. {#tbl-crosscorrelation}

Three choices distinguish it from the classic formulation (BrainVision
Analyzer's, for instance):

- **Each lag is normalised by the samples that overlap at that lag**, not by
  the whole segment, so every value is a true correlation between -1 and 1,
  and lags are comparable.
- **Trials are averaged in Fisher's *z***, $z = \operatorname{atanh} r$, and
  transformed back, since the mean of *r* is biased towards zero; this also
  gives the standard error drawn as a band.
- **Rejected samples are excluded pairwise, per lag**, and a lag with too few
  pairs is left empty rather than estimated from almost no data.

![The cross-correlation of FP1 with VEOG in one N400 bin: a negative peak at 0 ms, since eye activity appears with opposite signs in FP1 and in the bipolar VEOG channel.](images/crosscorrelation-result.jpg){#fig-crosscorrelation-result}

**Toolbox or own code.** MATLAB's `xcorr` normalises every lag by the whole
signals' energies. Cross Correlation reports a true correlation coefficient
at each lag, over the samples that overlap and were not rejected, which no
toolbox function computes, so it is checked against a direct per-lag
calculation instead.

## Source Estimate {#sec-tr-sourceestimate}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > Source Estimate · averaged →
averaged, with a stored source estimate · `SourceEstimate`*

Inverts every bin of an averaged dataset onto a template cortical surface
and stores the result on a node, so that a source cluster test
(@sec-source-cluster) and the 3D brain read it instead of computing it again.
The inverse methods and their limits are described in
@sec-source-estimation.

![**Source Estimate**: the inverse method, the orientation, the cortical mesh, the time window, the stored sampling rate and the regularisation, with the disk space the node will take.](images/sourceestimate-dialog.png){#fig-sourceestimate-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|--------------|------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| **Inverse method** | dSPM | **dSPM** [@dale2000] or **sLORETA** [@pascualmarqui2002]. |
| **Orientation** | Signed (cortical normal) | The dipole component along the cortical normal, keeping its sign, or the **Magnitude** of a free orientation. |
| **Source space** | 20 484 vertices | The template cortical mesh: 20 484, 8 196 or 5 124 vertices. |
| **Time window** | the whole epoch | The samples stored. |
| **Store at** | 200 Hz | The rate the estimate is stored at. |
| **Noise covariance** | From the baseline | What dSPM is normalised by: the baseline covariance Average stored, or **White noise (identity)** (@sec-noise-covariance). Only white noise is offered when the dataset carries no baseline covariance. |
| **Signal-to-noise ratio** | 3 | With the baseline covariance, sets the regularisation, λ = 1/SNR². |
| **Regularisation** | 0.05 | The Tikhonov regularisation with white noise, and for sLORETA. |

: Source Estimate's options. {#tbl-sourceestimate}

A stored estimate is reused only when every one of these settings, the
montage and the data themselves match what the later analysis needs, so they
should be the same for every subject. The dialog shows the space the node
will take, which for a fine mesh and a long window is much larger than a
typical node.

![The N400 difference at 400 ms as a dSPM estimate on the template cortex, drawn as a magnitude (the **Signed** box unticked). The fit line reports how much of the scalp data the estimate reproduces.](images/sourceestimate-result.jpg){#fig-sourceestimate-result}

## Source Regions {#sec-tr-sourceregions}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > Source Regions · averaged →
averaged, one channel per brain region · `SourceRegions`*

The time course of every region of an atlas: each bin is inverted onto the
template cortex exactly as Source Estimate does, with the same settings and
noise covariance, and the vertices of each region are averaged by
FieldTrip's `ft_sourceparcellate`. The atlas is one FieldTrip ships, AAL
[@tzourio2002] or Brainnetome [@fan2016]. The result is an averaged dataset
whose channels are regions, so the ERP plot, ERP Measure, grand averages,
the statistics reports and TimeFrequency all read it as they read
electrodes; its amplitude axis is the estimate's scale, not microvolts.

![**Source Regions**: the atlas, how a region's vertices are combined, and the source estimate's own settings.](images/sourceregions-dialog.png){#fig-sourceregions-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|--------------|------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| **Atlas** | AAL | The regions: AAL's or Brainnetome's, mapped onto the cortical sheet in MNI space by FieldTrip's `ft_sourceinterpolate` (nearest neighbour). A vertex in no region takes no part. |
| **Region value** | Mean magnitude | **Mean magnitude**: the mean of the vertices' magnitudes, always positive. **Signed mean**: the mean along the cortical normal, each vertex first turned to its region's dominant orientation, so the two banks of a sulcus do not cancel and an ERP's polarity survives (MNE's *mean_flip*). |
| **Inverse method** | dSPM | As in Source Estimate (@sec-tr-sourceestimate). |
| **Source space** | 20 484 vertices | As in Source Estimate. |
| **Noise covariance** | auto | **auto** uses the baseline covariance when the dataset has one (@sec-noise-covariance). |
| **Signal-to-noise ratio**, **Regularisation** | 3, 0.05 | As in Source Estimate. |

: Source Regions' options. {#tbl-sourceregions}

A region is only as distinct as the estimate under it. With a template head
and a few dozen electrodes, neighbouring regions share much of their signal
(@sec-source-estimation), so an effect larger in one region than in the next
is weak evidence that it is located there and not there.

![The N400 bins in the left middle temporal gyrus (AAL's Temporal_Mid_L), as a signed dSPM time course.](images/sourceregions-result.jpg){#fig-sourceregions-result}

## Dipole Fit {#sec-tr-dipolefit}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > Dipole Fit · averaged →
averaged, with the fitted dipoles · `DipoleFit`*

An equivalent current dipole, or a pair mirrored across the midline, fitted
to a bin's scalp distribution over a time window: where one focal generator
(or one in each hemisphere) would have to be to produce it, and how much of
the data it then explains. The fit is FieldTrip's `ft_dipolefitting`
[@oostenveld2011] on the template head model the source estimates use: a
grid search over the brain for the starting point, then a nonlinear fit.
The model holds the position fixed over the window and lets the moment
change within it (FieldTrip's *regional* model). The data are not changed;
the dipoles are stored with them, and the view draws them on a see-through
template brain with a table of their positions.

![**Dipole Fit**: the bins, the window, one dipole or a mirrored pair, and the spacing of the grid search.](images/dipolefit-dialog.png){#fig-dipolefit-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|--------------|------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| **Bins** | the first | The bins to fit, each on its own. |
| **From**, **To** | 20 ms either side of the largest global field power after the event | The window, in ms. |
| **Model** | One dipole | **One dipole**, or a **Mirrored pair**, symmetric across the midline, for a response from both hemispheres at once. |
| **Grid search spacing** | 10 mm | The grid the starting point is searched on. |
| **Optimiser** | FieldTrip's choice | The nonlinear fit's optimiser: FieldTrip's own choice, as in a FieldTrip script (`fminunc` where MATLAB reports the Optimization Toolbox, `fminsearch` otherwise), or **fminsearch**. |

: Dipole Fit's options. {#tbl-dipolefit}

The fit runs with FieldTrip's own defaults, as a FieldTrip script would. On
a MATLAB that reports the Optimization Toolbox without having all of it
installed, FieldTrip's choice, `fminunc`, stops with an error, and FieldTrip
returns only the grid search's starting point; Dipole Fit then refuses the
fit and says so. Choose **fminsearch** there.

A dipole is the right model only when one focal generator (or one in each
hemisphere) is a fair assumption, as for an early sensory response; it is
not the right model for a component with distributed generators, such as
the N400. The **residual variance**, the share of the scalp data in the
window the dipoles do not reproduce, is the check, and the view puts it in
the title. A low value says the model can explain the map, not that the
generator is where the dipole is: with a template head and template
electrode positions, a position is good to a centimetre or two. Each dipole
is named by the AAL region at or within 10 mm of it, by FieldTrip's
`ft_volumelookup`, since a fitted dipole often lies just beneath the cortex.

The example is an early sensory response: the visual response to the faces
in Ehinger and Dimigen's recording (@sec-deconvolution), in the plain
average of the **Stimulus** bin (454 trials), around its first peak at
102 ms, strongly positive over O1 and O2. From 82 to 122 ms a mirrored pair
lands in the calcarine cortex of each hemisphere, at ±24, -69, 4 mm, and
leaves 1.7% of the data unexplained. A single dipole over the same window
leaves only 2.4%, yet sits on the midline, in the cerebellar vermis, between
the two hemispheres' generators: the two models fit almost equally well,
and only one of them is where the visual cortex is.

![A mirrored pair fitted to the visual response to faces, 82 to 122 ms: one dipole in the calcarine cortex of each hemisphere, 1.7% of the data unexplained.](images/dipolefit-result.jpg){#fig-dipolefit-result}

## Beamformer {#sec-tr-beamformer}

*Tools > 4. Frequency and Component Analysis > Beamformer · epoched →
averaged, with a map of power change · `Beamformer`*

Where power changes between a baseline window and an active window of the
same length, at every location of a source model, by FieldTrip's
beamformers [@vanveen1997; @gross2001]. **LCMV** compares power in the time
domain, from the covariance of the trials; **DICS** compares power at one
frequency, from their cross-spectra, which suits an induced oscillation or a
frequency-tagged response. The result is the trials' average, as Average
makes it, with the map stored beside it; the view draws the map
(@sec-beamformers).

![**Beamformer**: the bins, the method and its frequency, the two windows, the source model and the regularisation.](images/beamformer-dialog.png){#fig-beamformer-dialog}

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|--------------|------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| **Bins** | every ordinary bin | The bins mapped; their trials together make the filter. |
| **Method** | LCMV | **LCMV (time domain)** or **DICS (frequency)**. |
| **Frequency**, **Smoothing** | 10 Hz, 4 Hz | DICS only: the frequency, and the multitaper smoothing around it. |
| **Active from/to**, **Baseline from/to** | 300 to 500, -200 to 0 ms | The two windows compared. They must be of the same length. |
| **Source model** | Cortical sheet | The template **Cortical sheet**, or a regular **Volume grid** inside the template brain. |
| **Sheet vertices** | 5 124 | The sheet: 5 124, 8 196 or 20 484 vertices. |
| **Grid spacing** | 10 mm | The grid. |
| **Regularisation** | 5 % | The diagonal loading of the covariance or cross-spectra, as a percentage of the mean sensor power, FieldTrip's `lambda`. |

: Beamformer's options. {#tbl-beamformer}

The value at each location is the relative change, (active - baseline) /
baseline, so 1 means the power doubled. A trial rejected anywhere in either
window takes no part; the view says how many did.

![LCMV power change from -200 to 0 ms to 300 to 500 ms in the N400 data, on the cortical sheet.](images/beamformer-result.jpg){#fig-beamformer-result}

![The same on a 10 mm volume grid, on slices of the template MRI through the peak.](images/beamformer-grid.jpg){#fig-beamformer-grid}
